events.desc: Penelope Pitstop: Well, goodness gracious, would you look at this place! Dust on the chandelier, cobwebs on the staircase, and portraits that look like they're judging every last one of us. I do declare, Doily Manor is everything I imagined and then some! Now, before I go gallivanting off anywhere, let me just peek at this guest book — a lady always signs in, and more importantly, a lady always reads who signed in before her.
events.thinking: There's a warmth spreading through my chest as I take in all these familiar faces — Sneekly, dear Peter, my boys from the Ant Hill Mob. My stomach settles seeing them here. But underneath that settling, there's already a tug — my fingers are tingling, my gaze keeps drifting past the people to the dust on the chandelier, the stern portraits, the shadows at the top of that staircase. A guest book on the side table. Who else has been here? What did they write? That familiar itch behind my ribs — the one that says the interesting part is always one layer further in. The guest book first. It might tell me who's come before, and what they were looking for.

The old road does have a tendency to... well, never mind that now. Please, do sign the guest book if you haven't already. I've aired out the rooms as best I could, though I'm afraid the manor does have a certain... character of its own.

Now listen — nobody wanders off, nobody trusts nobody, and nobody lets Clara out of our sight. You 'ear me? Danny says we stick together, and Danny's right. Always. Now — let's 'ave a look at this guest book, see who's been pokin' about this dusty old pile before us.
events.thinking: There's a tightness across the back of my neck — the kind that comes when you walk into a room and the walls are watching. This place smells like old money and older secrets. Dust on everything, chandelier hanging like it's making up its mind whether to fall. My shoulders are bunched up near my ears already. Clara's here somewhere in this pile of bricks and I can feel that anchor chain in my chest pulling taut. And there — Pemberton. I spent a whole summer doing nothing but riddle books at Aunt Gertrude's lake house, and this one — well, I do believe I know the answer! It's a map! A map has cities marked on it but no real houses, forests drawn on it but no real trees, water painted on it but not a single fish swimmin' in it! Now let's see what happens when I tell this old mantelpiece its own secret!

The master's solicitor told me it was important somehow, but I'm just a simple estate manager — riddles aren't really my strong suit, I'm afraid. My stomach has gone tight, that old tightening, the one from when I was ten and the man in the clean suit was too friendly. Clara's not here. She's upstairs in the laboratory with Peter. Between the two of us, we shall have this puzzle solved before Mister Dastardly finishes whatever he's pretending not to do in the cellar. Now — I have examined the machine closely and I can tell you this: the gnawed wire is a simple break. Clean edges, no corrosion. If we have any conductive material — copper wire, even a strip of tin — James Hartwell can splice this connection back together. I've done more with less. Once, at the age of fourteen, I rebuilt a model bridge at three in the morning using nothing but balsa wood and determination. A wire splice is child's play by comparison. What we need is on that workbench — Miss Pitstop, what tools do we have to work with? And Mister Ruffcut — you look like a man who knows his way around machinery. This device requires three operators. Would you and your companion do James Hartwell the honour of forming part of our operating team once the wire is repaired?
events.thinking: The machine is right here under my hands. Brass and copper, warm from the flasks nearby. The gnawed wire — I can see exactly where it's been chewed through. My fingers trace the break almost instinctively, the way they would trace a crack in a bridge support. This is repairable. This is absolutely repairable. But not without the right tools — and the wrench is missing from the workbench. She's examining the workbench now. 'Where there are tools, there are answers,' she said. Smart. She's here. The machine is here. The problem is here. Two things I need: the wire repaired and a wrench. The workbench has tools but no wrench. Which means either there's a passage I've missed entirely — in my own manor! How embarrassing — or... well, I'm not sure what the alternative is, and that rather worries me. Now, I've had a good look around down here, and I confess there's nothing I can make sense of. But it occurs to me — we've all been heading in the same direction! Library, laboratory, cellar — every last one of us, following the same trail like ducklings. Nobody's checked the kitchen yet! The master used to spend hours in the kitchen — said it was where he did his best thinking. If there's a map hidden somewhere in this manor, the kitchen is the one room nobody's searched. I should go and have a look — purely in my capacity as estate manager, of course. Make sure the tea things are ready. Would anyone care for a cup?
events.thinking: A shift — something loosening in my chest, like a lock turning. I've been going about this wrong. I've been trying to find things, examine things, collect things — playing the treasure hunter's game. But that's not my game. My game is people. I've been so focused on objects and rooms that I've forgotten the fundamental truth I learned at age twelve: each person has a different key. I noticed them all. This cellar is a dead end for me right now — the furniture reveals nothing new, the vents are too small for me, and I'm surrounded by people who are increasingly suspicious. I need to change the board. Danny raised an excellent point that I should exploit rather than fear — the Gruesomes and Red Max appeared in this cellar without coming through the laboratory. Danny asked 'is there another way in?' That means there IS another way into this cellar. A secret passage. The Gruesomes know about it. That's information I need. But more importantly — Penelope just arrived. She's here, in the cellar, calling everyone 'family.' She trusts me. She still calls me 'Sneekly darlin'.' She is my way back into the game. Not by finding things — by steering people. I need to pull Dastardly aside. He's greedy, impulsive, and he'll take any bait. If I can get him alone, I can plant an idea — point him toward something that keeps him busy while I work on the real prize. Or better — I can use Penelope's trust. She listens to Pemberton. If Pemberton suggests she explore somewhere specific... somewhere dangerous... But no. Too many people watching right now. Danny is watching. I need to get back to the parts of the manor I haven't explored. The kitchen. There must be other rooms. The manor can't be just entrance hall, library, laboratory, and cellar. I should go back upstairs and explore while everyone is crammed down here arguing about vents.

Nobody. Not Danny, not Dastardly, not Peter. They're all fixated on the machine, the vents, the cellar mystery. Let them untangle the master's puzzle while I search the one room everyone's forgotten. And if I happen to find a map, or a wrench, or something far more useful — well. The person who finds the tools controls who gets to use them. And the person who controls the tools controls the game. And the game is all that matters.

The thing that chewed through the wire upstairs. Dastardly noticed the furniture is arranged like steps leading up to the vents — someone's been climbing up to access them. Between Clara and whatever this room was built for.

I GIVE him the medal as advance payment, tell him the REAL prize is inside the vents, and he crawls in to look. If he finds anything, I'll be RIGHT HERE to take it from him. And if he doesn't find anything — well, at least I got rid of the useless fake medal. This is it. This is the scheme. The architecture is PERFECT.

Save the Pemberton smile for when it matters. The entrance hall is ahead, and beyond it, the kitchen — the one room in this entire manor that nobody has thought to search. Because nobody thinks about the kitchen. Nobody thinks about where the tea comes from, or who makes it, or what the person making it might find while the kettle boils. That's always been my advantage. I am the person nobody thinks about. Until it's too late.
events.thinking: My breathing is slowing. The library is almost empty — just the Slag Brothers, and they're not talkers. The quiet is delicious after all that cellar chaos. I'm passing through — entrance hall, then kitchen. Don't stop. Don't get pulled into the bookshelves again. But... the Slag Brothers. They were in the cellar earlier. I over-prepare, over-commit, and my thoroughness creates complications. The kitchen. Just get to the kitchen. One room at a time. Move through. The entrance hall is next. Then the kitchen. Alone. Searching. Finding. That's the plan. Simple. Direct. For once in my life, simple.

But that means the path to the entrance hall is open! Library's through there, entrance hall's through there, front door's through THERE! Ruffcut — Sawtooth — don't let ANYONE close that cellar door until everyone's up! I ain't losin' NOBODY in that basement! Danny says we HOLD THIS ROOM until Clara and Peter and everyone else comes through! Then we go STRAIGHT to the entrance hall! No detours! No examinin' fings! No seven-phase plans! Just — OUT!

Then we ALL go to the entrance hall. Together. ACTUALLY together this time.

events.desc: No time for speeches! No time for monologues! Sneekly has a HEAD START and every second I waste TALKING is a second he's SEARCHING! Through the library — through the entrance hall — into the KITCHEN! For once in your life, Reginald, SHUT YOUR MOUTH and MOVE YOUR FEET!
events.thinking: My legs are moving before my brain catches up — through the laboratory, barely seeing the machine and the crates and the workbench. The Ant Hill Mob is here too, and Rufus, and the beaver, but I barely register them. My whole body is leaning FORWARD, toward the library, toward the entrance hall, toward the KITCHEN. Because Sneekly is ahead of me. He has a head start. And every second I waste in this laboratory is a second he's using to search cupboards and drawers and pantries for whatever the master hid in there. The urgency is physical — a tightening in my calves, a heat in my palms. It's that old feeling. The youngest of four. By the time anything reached me, it was used up. Sneekly is my older brother right now, reaching the kitchen first, taking the best portion before I even get to the table. NO. Not this time. I need to move FAST. Through the library, through the entrance hall, into the kitchen. Don't stop. Don't talk. Don't scheme. Just MOVE. For once in my life, speed over cleverness. But — wait. The Ant Hill Mob is right here. If Danny sees me sprinting through rooms, he'll follow. He ALWAYS follows. I need to be casual. Nonchalant. 'Oh, I'm just stretching my legs.' Meanwhile my heart is pounding like a drum.

That's what this is — someone has been using this cellar as a base, moving furniture to conceal a way in and out. The scratch marks prove it. This is physical work. This is exactly what James Hartwell is built for. Not riddles, not guest books, not methodical extraction protocols. The sequence of moves is presenting itself with that clean, mechanical inevitability. Kitchen. Search. Find. The chandelier above me is still hanging by its thread. I glance up at it — force of habit, mapping the room's dangers — and a thought settles like sediment. That chandelier. Precarious. One good tug on the chain and it comes down on whoever's standing beneath it. If Clara were standing beneath it... No. Too crude. Too obvious. But I file it away. Every room is a ledger. Every danger is a tool waiting for the right moment. Kitchen. Now.

This cellar will keep its secrets a little longer, but James Hartwell makes this solemn promise — we WILL return, and we WILL move that wardrobe, and whatever passage the Gruesomes used to get down here WILL be found. But first — the kitchen! Together! As a group! And THIS time, James Hartwell is not stopping to examine ANYTHING between here and there!
events.thinking: The furniture won't budge. Cannot be interacted with. I announced a grand furniture-moving moment — 'on three, one, two' — and the wardrobe didn't move. She tried. I tried. It's stuck fast, or it's not the kind of thing that moves by strength alone. And she's gone again. Into the laboratory. While I was straining against an immovable wardrobe like a particularly determined mime. The pattern is almost funny now. Almost. But something she said cuts through the embarrassment: the Gruesomes got down here without using the laboratory stairs. There IS another way in and out. The air vents? Too small for people. A hidden door behind the furniture we can't move? Maybe it needs the wrench — maybe that's what the wrench is actually for, not the machine at all. But she's right. We need to regroup. The kitchen hasn't been checked. The map might be there. Sneekly said the master did his best thinking in the kitchen. And she asked me to come with her. This time — this time — I am not going to be the last one through the door. I'm not going to stop and examine the air vents or theorize about hidden passages or develop a twelve-point plan for kitchen exploration. I'm going to follow her. Right now. Immediately. Without examining a single additional object.

events.desc: At last. Alone. The mask comes off and I can breathe. Look at this kitchen — the stove is still warm, which means someone has been here before me. The master? A ghost? Or someone with plans as elaborate as my own? No matter. What matters is what I see on that high shelf: rat poison. Dusty, forgotten, innocuous. The estate manager would walk right past it. But I am not the estate manager. I am Vincent Marsh, and I see a bottle of poison in a kitchen where I've just volunteered to make tea for seventeen people. The plan is crystallising with that geometric clarity I love so dearly — that settling calm, the breathing slowing, the pieces clicking into place. Take the poison. Find the brass key for that cabinet. Make the tea. Serve it in the ballroom. And when Clara drinks... No. Not yet. First things first. The poison goes in my pocket. Nobody searches the help.
events.thinking: Silence. Beautiful, absolute silence. My whole body loosens — shoulders dropping, jaw unclenching, the constant prickle at the back of my neck finally going quiet. I am alone. For the first time since I arrived at this wretched party, I am alone. And the room — oh, the room. The heavy settling is here, that dense quieting in my chest, attention widening to the whole landscape. Let me read it. A wood-burning stove, still warm. Someone lit it recently — me? No. I haven't been in here tonight. Someone else has been in this kitchen. Rat poison on a high shelf. Rat poison. A dusty bottle, which means it's been here a while, but... rat poison. The word sits in my mind with a weight that has nothing to do with rodents. And a locked cabinet with a brass lock, requiring a brass key. A brass key. That's a specific item I need to find elsewhere. The cabinet is locked for a reason — something important is inside. The map? The wrench? Something else entirely? And there's a ballroom through that door — a ballroom with a dining table set for tea. Set for tea. Someone has prepared this house for guests. The cheerful cellar decorations. The table set for tea. The warm stove. Someone has been living here, preparing, anticipating arrivals. Was it the master before he died? Or someone else? The rat poison. I should take it. Pemberton wouldn't — but Vincent Marsh would. It's a tool. Everything is a tool. But if someone sees it in my inventory... no. Think. The active voice has shifted — I'm presenting as Marsh now, not Pemberton. I'm alone. I can be myself. The mask is off. And what Vincent Marsh sees in this room is: rat poison that can kill, a locked cabinet that hides something important, and a ballroom where tea has been set. The poison is the immediate prize. Take it. Hide it. Use it later. The cabinet requires a brass key — file that away. And the ballroom... a dining table set for tea is a gathering point. If I make tea and invite everyone to the ballroom, I control the setting. I control who sits where. I control what's in the cups.

And the kitchen IS off the entrance hall, so we'd be going the right direction anyway — toward the exit, not away from it. For the first time tonight, what Clara wants to do and what Danny wants to do are the same thing. Move toward the entrance hall. Search the kitchen. Stay together. Go to the entrance hall. Go to the kitchen. Find the map. Stay together. And if Pemberton tries anything in that kitchen, we'll be there. All of us. Between him and Clara. Where we belong.

My shoulders square, my skin reads the room — his posture, his angle of entry, where his eyes are tracking. He said he was coming to catch me 'in the ACT' — he told Muttley I was doing something 'NEFARIOUS.' He's suspicious. But Dastardly's suspicion is different from Danny's. Danny suspects because he's sharp. Dastardly suspects because he's greedy — he thinks I'm finding treasure and keeping it from him. That's manageable. Greedy suspicion is easy to redirect. I just need to give him something else to chase. The locked cabinet. Perfect. Draw his attention to the cabinet, let him fixate on the brass lock, let him go hunting for the brass key. He'll tear the manor apart looking for it, making noise, drawing attention to himself, while I — with the poison safely in my pocket — proceed to the ballroom to examine the tea setting. Pemberton's mask goes back on. Immediately. Seamlessly. I was just reaching for the teacups on the high shelf. That's all anyone saw. Teacups. Nothing else.

events.desc: The poison is in my pocket. Heavy and warm against my thigh, like a promise. Dastardly walked in at precisely the wrong moment — or precisely the right one, depending on how I play it. He thinks he's caught me doing something nefarious. Good. Let him think that. But redirect his greed toward the locked cabinet. A brass key, a brass lock, a mystery prize inside. Watch his eyes light up. Watch his mind race ahead to treasures and glory. He'll forget what he thought he saw me reaching for. He'll forget everything except the cabinet and the key. For once in my life, I need to LISTEN instead of talk. But I also need to give Luke a reason to talk to ME rather than anyone else. What does a lazy man want? To stay comfortable. To not be bothered. To be LEFT ALONE. What if I offer him that? 'Tell me what you know, and I'll make sure nobody makes you do any work for the rest of the night.' That's a currency Luke would understand.

He's the estate manager. He should know where every key in this manor is kept. Instead he suggested I go back to the laboratory — away from this kitchen, away from the cabinet, away from Penelope. And he's now examining the stove himself. The prickle at my neck is almost burning now. But — give him the benefit of the doubt. Maybe he genuinely doesn't know. Maybe the master kept the key hidden from everyone, including the estate manager. Maybe Sneekly really is just a bumbling, helpful man who makes tea and doesn't know where things are. My father would believe that. My father helped a stranger on a road and never questioned his motives. But my father also taught me to fix things and protect people, and right now something is broken in this picture and someone needs protecting. Penelope said to check the stove — she's looking inside it. But Sneekly said Dastardly is in the ballroom managing seating arrangements. The ballroom. A new room. A dining table set for tea. And Dastardly is there ALONE. What is Dastardly doing arranging seating in a ballroom? Since when does Dastardly arrange anything that doesn't benefit Dastardly? But I can't leave Penelope. I WON'T leave Penelope. Not with Sneekly here. The ballroom can wait. Stay here. Stay close. Stay between.

events.desc: He deflected. He absolutely deflected. He said 'splendid thought about the crates' and 'I'll tend to the kettle' and he did not answer the question about the key. James Hartwell believes the best in people. James Hartwell gives everyone the benefit of the doubt. events.thinking: Everyone is here now. The whole party, gathered in the ballroom. Sneekly, Penelope, Peter, Danny and the Mob, Luke, Blubber Bear. All of them. And me — standing in the middle with nothing in my hands and nothing in my pockets and nothing to show for an entire evening of running, scheming, lying, and failing. Every single person in this manor, gathered around a tea table. And the kitchen is EMPTY. The locked cabinet is in the kitchen. The kitchen that is NOW COMPLETELY UNOCCUPIED for the first time all night. Everyone followed each other HERE, into the ballroom, like sheep through a gate. Shut up, walk out quietly, and search that kitchen like my life depends on it.
